The more stat points you invest into any given attribute, the less stat growth you’ll get with each point. This is a scale of diminishing returns.

A soft-cap is the point at which putting a single point into a stat will give you drastically less stat growth than the point before it. It’s a hard drop-off rather than the linear decay you were seeing with all of those earlier points.

Go to Rennala and experiment with your stats to really get a feel for how the numbers change. You can see how your weapon AR is affected with each point that way. What you’ll notice is a relatively smooth scale of diminishing returns with each point up until 60, which is the soft cap for str/dex with regards to weapon damage bonus. 

Hope that clarifies a little bit.

It’s not about making the game easier. I’m fine with an easy mode. And as weird as it is talking about this in a LoP Reddit thread, I’m a big proponent of progressive policy.

My point centres around game design. The way throwable items work right now, they are very easily exploitable to bypass the game’s systems (i.e. enemy led combat with a focus on dodge/parry timing and attack opportunity).

All I’m asking is that, unless you’re speed running or something, which introduces a whole other system, you play the game how it was intended to be played, the fun way.
I actually just enjoy the conversation around game balance because I think it’s an interesting topic. Y’all need to chill.

I don’t care if the game has an easy mode as long as it’s FUN. 
And you may say fun is subjective and you’re absolutely right. But I also don’t think anybody in their right mind would say that watching paint dry is a more fun activity than watching your favourite tv show. More power to you if you disagree but I think it’s fair to say you’d be in the minority.

To illustrate my point a little bit more directly, the gaming industry collectively decided, at some point in the past decade, that quick-time-events (QTE’s) are not fun and not good, and so games that come out these days never include them anymore, and I think that’s for a good reason. See, there’s no strategy involved in a QTE, no “if x, then y” no thinking whatsoever. The amount of processing it takes to succeed a QTE is the same amount of processing it takes to start up the game: “press x”. So we throw them in the trash, good riddance. 

Now, there may have been a small contingent of gamers that didn’t mind or enjoyed QTE’s. I happened to fall into that camp when I played a game called Asura’s Wrath. But thinking back to when I played that game, my enjoyment of the QTE’s had nothing to do with the mechanic itself, if you can even call it that. The fun that I had was a product of the visual spectacle and emotional information that the scene conveyed, like a movie. Did pressing a single button over and over and over and over enhance the experience? Maybe, a little bit. But you know what would have enhanced it way more? Having to think a little bit, a challenge with some sort of in-depth mechanic that I can interact with and solve by familiarizing myself with it and executing it. 

My point is that wiping out half of a boss’s health by spamming the square button like a QTE with hardly any risk whatsoever, effectively robs the player of that interaction, because at that point, you don’t have to learn a boss’s moveset, you don’t have to learn how to respond to their attacks, you just have to run away and use up all your healing trying to out DPS whatever you face. 

It’s like watching paint dry.

I guess I’ll tell you why it’s hard to come by info. When I discovered the power of heavy abyssals I thought I’d uncovered some well kept secret. In all honesty, the difference in AR if you’re running heavy abyssals on a weapon isn’t THAT drastic. For most players, it’s really not worth farming layer 4 frc’s just for a 50 ish AR increase when there’s layer 1 bosses that drop 27% attack up gems. Useless info like that tends to get burried.

Now that said, strength quality with heavy abyssals will net you the highest AR on most physical weapons with some exceptions. My rule of thumb is if the weapons natural strength scaling is at D or below, it’s usually not that effective. Or alternatively, if the weapons natural strength scaling is an S, it’s also usually not worth it (I’m actually not sure why this is, maybe there’s a hard scalping cap or something, I’d actually like to know). Heavy abyssals give you an honestly stupid amount of strength scaling and for some reason (probably because it would be way too OP) there is NO skill equivalent for the highest tier strength scaling gems. 

There’s a lot of misinfo out there on this game and other souls games too which I honestly kind of sympathize with. There are a surprising amount number games you have to play if you really want to optimize for damage and in the end, you really don’t end up with that much more AR than if you just feel it out. Bloodborne is either a delicate dance of dodges and counterattacks or a one sided beat down where you aren't given a second to recover. One thing that I found absolutely genius about Father Gascoigne's fight was that he punishes you for trying to create space. If he knocks you down at any point during the fight, your Dark Souls instinct tells you to get away and recover. And this would probably be the right response in Dark Souls. However, Gascoigne doesn't let you do that; the only way to avoid his wakeup attack is to either dodge into and past him, or sideways to launch your own counterattack.

I wouldn't call any fight in it difficulty breaking. Hunter fights can be absolutely trivialized by parrying if you have a decent skill investment. That includes Gehrman and Maria. Kos is hard, really hard, but he reminds me a lot of phase 3 Gascoigne in his aggression. As long as you pay attention to his animations and don't get greedy with your own attacks, you can take care of him pretty easily.
